nameStory: The 'sessile-fruited' part of this plant's name comes from a botanical term meaning 'attached directly without a stalk.' Unlike many of its relatives, this arrowhead's female flowers sit right against the stem rather than dangling on little stalks. It's also called Canadian arrowhead because it's especially common in Canada's wetlands.
description: Sessile-fruited arrowhead is an aquatic plant that might surprise you - despite its name, it doesn't have the classic arrow-shaped leaves you'd expect! Instead, this wetland dweller sports narrow, oval leaves that emerge from shallow water. It produces charming white flowers with three petals on sturdy stalks above the water surface, and like its relatives, it grows edible potato-like tubers underground.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow oval leaves rather than arrow-shaped - this is the big surprise! They feel smooth and somewhat thick, emerging directly from the water on long stalks.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Three crisp white petals arranged in a simple, open face about the size of a quarter. Female flowers sit directly against the stem without stalks (hence 'sessile').

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Grows in shallow water with leaves and flower stalks poking up above the surface. Forms colonies connected by underground runners.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Female flowers develop into small, rounded clusters of seeds that sit tight against the flowering stem without dangling.

habitat: Look for this aquatic plant in shallow waters along pond edges, quiet stream margins, and marshy areas throughout New England. It prefers muddy or sandy bottoms in water that's typically 6 inches to 2 feet deep. You'll often find it growing alongside cattails, pickerelweed, and other water-loving plants.

seasonality.spring: New leaves begin emerging from the water as temperatures warm, starting as tightly rolled shoots that unfurl into their distinctive oval shape.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering time with bright white blooms standing above the water surface. This is when the plant is most visible and easiest to identify.
seasonality.fall: Leaves begin to yellow and die back, while underground tubers reach their peak size and energy storage for winter survival.
seasonality.winter: Completely dormant with no visible above-ground parts. The plant survives as tubers buried in the muddy bottom sediments.

funFact: This plant produces edible tubers that taste like potatoes when cooked, and Indigenous peoples have harvested them for thousands of years - but modern foragers beware, as the tubers can concentrate pollutants from contaminated water, making them potentially dangerous to eat in polluted areas!
confusionNotes: Most people expect all arrowheads to have arrow-shaped leaves, so this one throws everyone off! If you see white three-petaled flowers over water but oval leaves instead of arrows, you've likely found sessile-fruited arrowhead. Remember: 'sessile-fruited = not the typical arrowhead shape.'
contextualKnowledge: The name 'arrowhead' for this whole plant family comes from the classic arrow-shaped leaves of the most common species, broadleaf arrowhead. But several species in this genus break the mold with different leaf shapes, making the family name somewhat misleading for species identification.
compareHints: Unlike broadleaf arrowhead with its iconic three-pointed arrow leaves, sessile-fruited arrowhead has narrow ovals. It differs from grass-leaved arrowhead by having broader, more substantial leaves rather than thin, grass-like blades. The key identifier across all arrowheads is those distinctive three white petals and the aquatic habitat.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Broadleaf arrowhead stands out from its relatives by having the widest, most pronounced arrow-shaped leaves in the genus - while grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, strap-like leaves and slender arrowhead has thin, linear foliage.
Among New England's arrowheads, grass-leaved arrowhead is instantly recognizable by its narrow, grass-like leaves – all other species have distinctly arrow-shaped or oval leaves.
While broadleaf arrowhead has classic arrow-shaped leaves and grass-leaved arrowhead has broader, ribbon-like foliage, slender arrowhead's leaves are so narrow they look like green needles.
Compared to the common broadleaf arrowhead, Midwestern arrowhead has more narrow, elongated leaf lobes and distinctly shorter beaks on its fruits.
Among New England's arrowheads, arumleaf arrowhead is distinguished by its relatively broad, triangular leaves that are wider than they are long.
Among the arrowhead family, Engelmann's stands out for its extremely narrow leaf lobes and strict preference for acidic water.
Among New England's arrowheads, Spongy Arrowhead is distinguished by its uniquely soft, air-filled leaf stalks - a feature no other local Sagittaria species shares.
Among New England arrowheads, delta arrowhead has broader, more triangular leaves than the common broadleaf arrowhead, and much wider leaves than the grass-like narrow-leaved arrowhead.
Among New England's arrowheads, this species stands out for having the thinnest, most grass-like leaves - much narrower even than grass-leaved arrowhead.

Among New England arrowheads, hooded arrowhead is unique for its curved sepals that hood over the flower petals, while broadleaf arrowhead has flat, open flowers and grass-leaved arrowhead has narrow, grass-like leaves rather than the broad arrow shape.
